title: Toughest Game Yet!! Danya Is Sweating?!! | Halloween Gambit | The Sensei Speedrun | GM Naroditsky

moves.spoken: We play e5 again, staying with classical openings.
White develops a knight to f3.
We answer a knight to c6.
A knight to c3 — the Four Knights, not my favorite to face.
We develop the knight to f6.
And White throws in a knight capture on e5 — the Halloween Gambit, actually not a bad line and under-covered in books.
We accept, recapturing on e5. We'll play a variation that dodges most of the theory.

White plays d4. The engine's best is to keep the extra piece — retreat the knight to c6, meet e5 with a knight tucked back to g8, and White lacks full compensation — but I'm out of my depth there and suspect our opponent has analyzed it.
So we play a knight to g6 — not to keep the piece, but to give it back.
White pushes e5. The good thing about facing a gambit when you're unsure is that you can always hand the piece back and cash in on development instead.
We don't even move the f6 knight — a bishop to b4 develops as if nothing's the matter.
White captures on f6.

We recapture with the queen. I can't believe Black could be worse here — and gambit players hate a line where you sacrifice the piece back and drain the life out of the position. We'll play a solid, positional style, aiming a later queen to e6 to open lines toward f2.
A classic standoff of queens — you don't want to be the one to release the tension and help your opponent develop, so we won't take on e2; we develop and castle instead.
We recapture on e6 with the d-pawn — it opens the d-file and gives our light-squared bishop air, whereas the f-pawn recapture would leave that bishop boxed in behind pawns on d7 and e6.
White castles long.
A bishop to d7. The position is completely equal — we win it by patience, developing our pieces first.
White plays a3.
We trade on c3 — most people wouldn't, but this has a lot of venom.
White recaptures on c3, and now he's left without a knight in this type of position.
A bishop to c6, onto the long diagonal — the point is that White's bishop on c3 is a bad piece, and we'll launch a campaign against it.
White plays a rook to g1.
A rook to d8. Our plan is to pile on the d4 pawn — double the rooks and reroute the knight to f5, and before long d4 becomes a sitting duck.
White plays g3.
We start doubling with a rook to d7. We'll speed up, since our opponent is playing fast and confidently, but the pressure keeps building.
White plays a bishop to h3. Still equal — and knowing how to outplay strong players from such positions is an essential skill.
A rook to d8, completing the doubling — I don't see what the bishop threatens, so we continue the plan.
White plays a rook to e1.
Now it's time to reroute the knight to e7, heading for d5 or f5.
White plays f4. A knight to d5 might run into f5, so we think carefully.

A very good move is h5, stopping g4 and making it impossible for White to push f5 — a light-square blockade. It looks passive, but it freezes White's pawns; then g6 makes his kingside pawns immobile, and a capture on e6 is nothing to fear since we recapture and White loses his light-squared bishop. Our structure is watertight.
White plays b3. What I want is the c6 square for the knight — it would press d4 even harder. A knight to d5 is a dead end; c6 is the dream.
A bishop to f3 would allow a rook to d3 with tempo, so instead we build a home for the bishop with b6 and drop it back to b7, freeing the knight to reach c6.
White plays c4 — this also lets us push c5 if needed.
We play a knight to c6. White was almost lost but survives with a rook to e4 — very fortunate for him.
White plays a rook to e4. Maybe repeating and rerouting the knight to f5 is a better approach — and d5 could be unpleasant.
A rook to d6. Maybe the h5-and-g6 plan was a mistake, since it weakened the dark squares — I underestimated that, and now we have to spin our way out.
I'm quite concerned about d5 here — I'd totally forgotten it was an idea. We have to be careful not to get mated, but we have resources.
A knight to a5 was my initial idea, and against this very strong player, let's play it.
White plays a bishop to f6. There's a back-rank idea, so we always have to keep a rook guarding the eighth rank, which really limits us. We need to calculate carefully here.
We have to play the capture on d5.
White captures on d8.
We recapture on e4.
White takes on d6.
We recapture on d6. The good thing is that our knight on a5 is a monster, hitting b3.
White plays a king to c2. The knight on a5 gives us a tempo — we can push toward promotion, bring the king to f8, or play the f5 I like, which solidifies the whole pawn chain.
We play a king to f8 — the drawback is a bishop to f6, but it's better than nothing.
White plays a bishop to f6 — incredible tactics for White.
We bring the king closer with a king to e8.
And if the king comes to c3, we'll play d5.
We're playing for a win a pawn up, but White's bishops are strong and he has a lot of time — this will be a real challenge.
A knight back to c6 — now I'm concerned about b5.
White plays a4.
Let's play e3 — inducing b5 has an upside: it fixes the pawns on light squares, so if the king moves away we can play a bishop to b3.
White plays b5. I wouldn't say I'm in trouble — probably equal, but hard to win with Black despite our extra passed pawn on e3.
A knight to e7. If White now plays the king to d4 or d3, we have a bishop to b3. What worries me is a5, a high-level move to shatter our queenside.
White plays a bishop to e5, also very strong, eyeing b8.
It's time for e2 and a bishop to b3 — a bailout.
White plays a king to d2. We can try a bishop to c4, an ambitious try.
We play a bishop to b3. If White plays a bishop to b8 and takes, we can't win — but I see no alternative.
Very well played by my opponent. Let's try a knight to d5.
There are still tricks, but the problem is a bishop to g2 — one more trick up my sleeve.
He plays perfectly right up to the last, then blunders a piece — but this is far from over.
White plays a king to f3.
I apologize for the sparse explanation — I really need to focus to win this.
Even up a piece it's hard — the pawn on b5 ties us down.
h3 is another mistake, because we drop back to e7 attacking the bishop.
We'll take on h3 next and be up a full piece — but I have no time, so it's a tall order.
White plays f6 with check.
It should be a bishop to f5 — we complete that anyway.
Maybe not the cleanest way I'm playing this, but a knight to f6, heading for e4.
We go here to stop the pawn.
The point is that after b7 we stop it with a king to c7.
Now we take on g3 and simply push the h-pawn home.
And we win — probably the closest speedrun game we've had.

This guy is clearly legit — an amazingly played game. I'm honestly not proud of my level of play: a couple of misjudgments and flat-out misses, which makes it instructive because I can explain what I missed.
It's late and I'm running low, but I'll shed light on what happened. I've never faced the Halloween Gambit, so I never studied it properly.
I was afraid to play the knight to g8...
...because there's a good amount of theory there, and the engine gives about minus one and a half for Black.
It looks like a bishop to c4 is the line.
And now you're supposed to sacrifice one of the pawns back with d5.
You do that to open the center and develop more effectively.
d5 is a very common idea in these positions — sac a pawn back...
...and after a bishop capture on d5, two games went c6, a bishop to b3...
...and a bishop to b4, where it's fairly obvious White has insufficient compensation.
White has two pawns for the piece, but we control all the light squares.
Even if White plays f4 — the engine likes h5...
...similar to the game — we plant the bishop into f5 and totally dominate the light squares, so White can never push f5.
But we chose to give the piece back, which I think is a valid approach even though the engine doesn't love it.
If you give the piece back, after a knight to c6 and e5...

...maybe the way we did it wasn't best. In retrospect White's queen to e2 was strong, because otherwise we castle and play d5 with dead-equal play. Square control isn't abstract here: the point of controlling f5 is to stop White from playing f5 and rolling us off the board, and controlling g4 stops g4 — concrete purposes, not theory.
